paras: The threatened lynching of Dick Lee took place at Stanford, Kentucky, in late August 1910, when friends of two white men Lee was accused of stabbing at Moreland talked of storming the jail at Stanford to lynch him. No attempt was made, and Lee was held in jail for the grand jury.

The two men, named by the Stanford Interior Journal as Emmett Netkirk and Huston Acre, came from the Green river section of Casey County. According to the paper, which gave the account as hearsay, they had come to Moreland to seek work loading lumber, "much of which had been done by the negroes."

On Friday, 26 August, Lee was said to have become angry and "went after" the two men with a large knife when they resented remarks he had made to them, stabbing both. Sheriff W. L. McCarty arrested him that day and lodged him in the county jail at Stanford. That night, the Interior Journal reported, there was talk among the men's friends "of making an effort to storm the jail here that night and lynch the negro," but "cooler heads prevailed" and nothing was done.

Lee was brought before County Judge Bailey in the following days and held to await the action of the grand jury. His bond was set at $500, which he could not give, so he stayed in jail; Attorney T. J. Hill was retained to defend him. By then the two men, now called Akers and Neikirk, had recovered enough to appear against him.

Three weeks later the Adair County News identified the prisoner as Dick Lee Hardin, a "negro boy" born and reared near Columbia who had left after getting into trouble there six or eight years before. His mother, who lived near Columbia, was understood to have gone to Stanford to see him. No report of the grand jury's action or of a trial was found in the coverage through September.

The episode was covered only by Kentucky weeklies, and the lynching talk appears in just one of them. The Interior Journal headlined its first item "Mob Talk" and "Heard When Negro Stabbed White Men at Moreland," describing Lee as "a bad colored man" said to have "a bad reputation" and a "ready knife." Its follow-up, "Stays In Jail," ran on two pages of the 2 September issue and joked that Lee was "the guest of Col. Dink Farmer," while the paper's Hustonville correspondent praised "our most efficient sheriff" for the arrest.
The Adair County News took up the case only to answer a query from the Wayne County Outlook about who the prisoner was, and did not mention the threat. No coverage in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Dick Lee
bases: Friends of two white men Lee was accused of stabbing talked of storming the jail to lynch him, but nothing was done (A1); a threatened lynching.

Lee was not killed: the talk of storming the jail to lynch him came to nothing and he was held for the grand jury (A1, A2). The threat itself was extralegal and rested on the stabbing accusation, but no group is reported to have gathered.

The threat of lynching is reported only by the Stanford Interior Journal (A1); its follow-ups (A2, A5) and the Adair County News (A6) confirm the stabbing charge and jailing but do not mention the mob talk.

accounts.label: Stanford Interior Journal (local)
accounts.gist: Lee stabbed two white men who had come to Moreland seeking lumber-loading work done by Black men, after they 'resented his remarks'; their friends talked of storming the jail to lynch him, but cooler heads prevailed. The motive is given as 'it is said'.

accounts.label: Adair County News
accounts.gist: Identifies the arrested 'negro boy' as Dick Lee Hardin of the Columbia area, who had 'got into trouble here' and left six or eight years earlier.

framing.detail: The Interior Journal headlined the item 'Mob Talk' and reported the lynching talk without endorsing it, noting 'Cooler heads prevailed', while calling Lee 'a bad colored man' with 'a bad reputation' and a 'ready knife'.
The follow-up 'Stays In Jail' reported the court proceedings with a jocular line that Lee was 'the guest of Col. Dink Farmer'.
The Adair County News answered a Wayne County Outlook query about who Lee was, giving his full name and origins.

conflicts.note: Same paper, three days apart; spelling or OCR variants of the same two men.
The Adair County News gives a fuller name; not a contradiction.
